message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.).
• The property must meet all local health and safety codes. | • Document problems with photos, videos, or written notes.
• Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) and give a reasonable time to fix. | | **Repair & Maintenance** | • If the landlord fails to repair, you may:
1. **Withhold rent** (only after giving notice and following the proper procedure).
2. **Repair and deduct** (pay for the repair yourself and deduct the cost from rent).
3. **Terminate the lease** if the issue is serious (e.g., lack of heat, water, or major structural problems). | • Keep receipts and a written record of all communications.
• If you choose to repair, get a written estimate from a licensed contractor. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, the landlord can raise rent at the end of each month, but must give **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent can only increase at the start of a new term unless the lease allows it. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses.
• Ask for a written notice if you’re unsure. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies.
• “Reasonable” means a time that is convenient for both parties, not an arbitrary hour. | • Keep a log of all entries.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry and document the incident. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to privacy in your rented space.
• The landlord cannot monitor your activities or install surveillance without your consent. | • Report any unauthorized monitoring to the landlord in writing. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Eviction** | • The landlord must provide a **written notice** (usually 3 days for nonpayment, 30 days for lease violations, 60 days for no‑cause termination of month‑to‑month).
• The landlord cannot evict you without following the legal process. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, file a **motion to dismiss** in the county court. | | **Lease Termination** | • You can terminate a lease early if the landlord breaches the lease (e.g., fails to maintain habitability).
• Some leases allow early termination with a fee or notice. | • Provide written notice and keep copies. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities.
• If utilities are included, the landlord must keep them operational. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases require landlord approval for sublets or assignments.
• Texas law does not prohibit subletting, but the landlord can deny it if the lease says so. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Record Keeping** | • Keep copies of the lease, rent receipts, communication with the landlord, and any repair records. | • Store documents in a safe place; consider digital backups. | --- #### Quick Steps If You Encounter a Problem 1. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notes, receipts, and copies of all correspondence. 2. **Notify the Landlord in Writing** – Send a certified letter or email with a read receipt. Keep a copy. 3. **Give Reasonable Time** – Usually 30 days for repairs, 24 hours for entry. 4. **Seek Mediation** – Many counties offer free mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. 5. **File a Complaint** – If unresolved, file with TCHR, HUD, or the local housing agency. 6. **Legal Action** – As a last resort, file a lawsuit in the county court. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Property Code** | The statutory framework for landlord‑tenant relations. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** | Handles discrimination complaints. | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Handles federal fair housing complaints. | | **Local County Clerk’s Office** | Provides information on filing small claims or eviction motions. | | **Texas Legal Services** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance for qualifying tenants. | | **Tenant Rights Hotline** | Many counties have a dedicated hotline for tenant questions. | --- #### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, fair treatment, and protection against unlawful eviction or discrimination. Knowing the specific statutes and having a clear lease agreement will help you assert those rights effectively. If you’re ever unsure, consult a local attorney or tenant advocacy group.
